externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps the client’s address but splits traffic by node, not by pod

A Service of type LoadBalancer: a cloud load balancer sends outside requests to the nodes, and rules that kube-proxy writes on each node hand every request to a pod. Node 1 runs 3 pods, Node 2 runs 1 and Node 3 runs none. The setting chooses externalTrafficPolicy: Local.

Transcript

externalTrafficPolicy: Local · Pods on nodes 1, 2, 3: 3, 1, 0

  1. 4 pods on three nodes behind one load balancer

    A Service of type LoadBalancer: a cloud load balancer sends outside requests to the nodes, and rules that kube-proxy writes on each node hand every request to a pod. Node 1 runs 3 pods, Node 2 runs 1 and Node 3 runs none. The setting chooses externalTrafficPolicy: Local.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges:
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • 4 labelled values:
      • externalTrafficPolicy: Local;
      • Pods on nodes 1, 2, 3: 3, 1, 0;
      • Client address: 198.51.100.79;
      • kube-proxy mode: iptables, the Linux default.
  2. Under Local, each node’s rules list only its own pods

    In iptables mode kube-proxy writes one rule per pod. Rule i of n matches with probability 1/(n−i), and the last always matches, so each pod gets 1/n. Under Local Node 1 lists only its 3 pods: 1/3, 1/2, always, so each gets 1/3 of what Node 1 receives.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges:
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 (chain shown);
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • Code, 4 lines:
      • 1: # KUBE-SVL chain on Node 1, one rule per pod;
      • 2: -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.3333333333 -j pod a;
      • 3: -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.5000000000 -j pod b;
      • 4: -j pod c.
    • “Share of the node’s requests”, 3 labelled values:
      • Pod a: 1/3;
      • Pod b: 1/3;
      • Pod c: 1/3.
  3. Node 3 runs no pod, so it fails the health check

    Under Local, kube-proxy answers the load balancer’s health check on each node: 200 when the node runs a pod of the Service, 503 when it runs none. The load balancer stops sending to Node 3, so Node 1 and Node 2 each get 1/2 of the requests.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges:
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3 (fails the health check);
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • “Health check answer”, 3 labelled values:
      • Node 1: 200, 3 local pods;
      • Node 2: 200, 1 local pod;
      • Node 3: 503, 0 local pods.
  4. The request stays on its node and keeps the client’s address

    Node 1’s rules list only its own pods, so the request never leaves Node 1, and kube-proxy adds no source NAT for it. Pod a sees the client’s address, 198.51.100.79. Under Local no outside request takes a second hop.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges:
      • “from 198.51.100.79” beside Pod a (note);
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 (travelled);
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a (travelled);
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • 3 labelled values:
      • Client sends from: 198.51.100.79;
      • Pod a sees: 198.51.100.79;
      • Second hop: none.
  5. Pod d gets 1/2 of the requests; pods a, b and c get 1/6 each

    The load balancer splits by node, not by pod: Node 1 and Node 2 each get 1/2. Node 1 splits its 1/2 three ways; Node 2 sends all of its 1/2 to pod d, so pod d gets 3 times as many requests as pod a.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges:
      • “16.7%” beside Pod a (note);
      • “16.7%” beside Pod b (note);
      • “16.7%” beside Pod c (note);
      • “50%” beside Pod d (note);
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • “Share of all requests under Local”, 2 labelled values:
      • Pod d: 1/2 (50%);
      • Pods a, b and c: 1/6 each (16.7%).
  6. With 3, 1, 0 pods, Local trades even load for the client’s address

    Cluster spreads requests evenly over the pods, but 2 in 3 cross to another node and every pod sees a node’s address. Local keeps each request on its node with the client’s address. The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods, so pod d takes 3 times the load of pod a.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges:
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • “Cluster”, 3 labelled values:
      • Pods a, b, c and d: 1/4 each (25%);
      • Second hop: 2 in 3;
      • Pod sees: node address.
    • “Local”, 4 labelled values:
      • Pod d: 1/2 (50%);
      • Pods a, b and c: 1/6 each (16.7%);
      • Second hop: none;
      • Pod sees: client address.
  7. What these shares leave out

    The shares are long-run averages for kube-proxy’s iptables mode; IPVS mode defaults to round robin. kube-proxy’s health check reports each node’s pod count in a header, but the docs warn that some cloud load balancers cannot weight nodes. Topology-aware routing and session affinity are left out.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges:
      • the rest as in the previous step.
    • 5 labelled values:
      • Mode: iptables; IPVS uses round robin;
      • Load balancer: equal share per healthy node;
      • Health check header: X-Load-Balancing-Endpoint-Weight;
      • Topology-aware routing: not modelled;
      • Session affinity: not modelled.

      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • Code, 5 lines:
      • 1: # KUBE-SVC chain on every node, one rule per pod;
      • 2: -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.2500000000 -j pod a;
      • 3: -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.3333333333 -j pod b;
      • 4: -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.5000000000 -j pod c;

      • Pod a: 1/4;
      • Pod b: 1/4;

  3. Under Cluster, 2 in 3 requests leave the node they reach

    Each node gets a third of the requests and picks among all 4 pods. A request leaves its node when the pick runs elsewhere: 1 in 4 on Node 1, 3 in 4 on Node 2, all on Node 3. Here Node 3 sends one to pod d on Node 2.

      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3 (travelled);
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3 → Pod d (travelled);

      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;

      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • “Requests sent on to another node”, 4 labelled values:
      • Leave Node 1: 1 in 4;
      • Leave Node 2: 3 in 4;
      • Leave Node 3: all;
      • All requests: 2 in 3.
  4. The pod sees the node’s address, not the client’s

    Under Cluster, kube-proxy marks every outside request for source NAT, in case it crosses nodes. Node 3 replaces the client’s address, 198.51.100.79, with its own, 10.240.0.3, and pod d sees that. Requests that stay on their node are rewritten too.

      • Client sends from: 198.51.100.79;
      • Pod d sees: 10.240.0.3.
  5. Each pod gets 1/4 of the requests

    The load balancer gives each node 1/3, and each node’s rules give each of the 4 pods 1/4 of that. Summed over the three nodes, each pod gets 1/4 of all requests, wherever it runs.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 8 edges:
      • “25%” beside Pod a (note);
      • “25%” beside Pod b (note);
      • “25%” beside Pod c (note);

      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • “Share of all requests under Cluster”, 1 labelled value:
      • Pods a, b, c and d: 1/4 each (25%).
  6. With 3, 1, 0 pods, Local trades even load for the client’s address

    Cluster spreads requests evenly over the pods, but 2 in 3 cross to another node and every pod sees a node’s address. Local keeps each request on its node with the client’s address. The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods, so pod d takes 3 times the load of pod a.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 8 edges:
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3 → Pod d;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod b;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod c;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • “Cluster”, 3 labelled values:
      • Pods a, b, c and d: 1/4 each (25%);
      • Second hop: 2 in 3;
      • Pod sees: node address.
    • “Local”, 4 labelled values:
      • Pod d: 1/2 (50%);
      • Pods a, b and c: 1/6 each (16.7%);
      • Second hop: none;
      • Pod sees: client address.
  7. What these shares leave out

    The shares are long-run averages for kube-proxy’s iptables mode; IPVS mode defaults to round robin. kube-proxy’s health check reports each node’s pod count in a header, but the docs warn that some cloud load balancers cannot weight nodes. Topology-aware routing and session affinity are left out.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 8 edges:
      • the rest as in the previous step.
    • 5 labelled values:
      • Mode: iptables; IPVS uses round robin;
      • Load balancer: equal share per healthy node;
      • Health check header: X-Load-Balancing-Endpoint-Weight;
      • Topology-aware routing: not modelled;
      • Session affinity: not modelled.

externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster · Pods on nodes 1, 2, 3: 2, 2, 0

  1. 4 pods on three nodes behind one load balancer

    A Service of type LoadBalancer: a cloud load balancer sends outside requests to the nodes, and rules that kube-proxy writes on each node hand every request to a pod. Node 1 runs 2 pods, Node 2 runs 2 and Node 3 runs none. The setting chooses externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster.

    • Architecture diagram: 8 services, 8 edges:
      • Load balancer;
      • Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;
      • Load balancer → Node 2 · 10.240.0.2;
      • Load balancer → Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3;
      • Node 3 · 10.240.0.3 → Pod d;
      • Node 1 · 10.240.0.1;

      • Node 2 · 10.240.0.2 → Pod d;
      • Pod a;
      • Pod b;
      • Pod c;
      • Pod d.
    • 4 labelled values:
      • externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster;
      • Pods on nodes 1, 2, 3: 2, 2, 0;
      • Client address: 198.51.100.79;
      • kube-proxy mode: iptables, the Linux default.
  2. Each node’s rules pick one of all 4 pods

    In iptables mode kube-proxy writes one rule per pod. Rule i of n matches with probability 1/(n−i), and the last always matches, so each pod gets 1/n. Under Cluster every node lists all 4 pods: 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, always, so each gets 1/4 of what the node receives.
